vignette:
Alex describes his life now as living in grayscale. This is particularly poignant coming from a man who once built his career on a mastery of color theory and vibrant design. At 33, he works from a spare bedroom in a quiet suburban apartment, a self-imposed exile from the bustling downtown agency he once loved. The tools of his trade—a high-resolution monitor, a graphics tablet, a meticulously calibrated Pantone swatch book—surround him, but the creative spark he once took for granted feels distant, like a memory from someone else’s life.

Four years ago, that life was his. He was married to Sarah, living in a trendy loft, and was on track for a promotion to Art Director. The trauma arrived without warning on a Tuesday night. It wasn't a car crash or a combat zone; it was the splintering of his own front door. He and Sarah had been hosting a small get-together for a friend’s birthday. The music was a little loud, but not excessively so. The next thing he knew, the room was filled with shouting, blinding flashlights, and the terrifying presence of several police officers in tactical gear, responding to a mistaken report of a violent crime at their address.

Alex remembers the confusion more than the fear, at first. He remembers trying to explain, to ask what was happening, only to be shoved against the wall. He can still feel the cold, metallic bite of the handcuffs and the rough, unforgiving texture of the pavement against his cheek after he was forced to the ground on the sidewalk outside his own building. He was held for hours, questioned aggressively, and treated not as a citizen, but as a suspect. The charges were eventually dropped, a clerical error was blamed, and a cursory apology was issued. But the damage was cellular. The world was no longer a fundamentally safe place.

In the months that followed, Alex tried to "get over it." He told himself it was a fluke, a crazy story to tell one day. But his body kept the score. A siren wailing three blocks away is enough to make his heart hammer against his ribs and his palms sweat, forcing him to pause his work and take deep, shuddering breaths. He quit his agency job six months after the incident. The daily commute, the casual police presence downtown, and the unpredictable noises of the city became an insurmountable gauntlet. Freelancing from home seemed like the only solution.

His relationships frayed. Sarah, his ex-wife, had tried to understand. But his irritability, his hair-trigger startle response, and his emotional numbness built a wall between them. He would lash out over small things, like a dish left in the sink, the rage feeling entirely disconnected from the trigger. He stopped wanting to go out, avoiding crowds and any situation he couldn’t immediately control. Intimacy became impossible; he couldn’t stand being touched unexpectedly and would often wake up thrashing from nightmares of being pinned down, tangled in his own sheets. The divorce was finalized last year. He says he doesn’t blame her; he knows he became a ghost in his own home.

Now, his days have a rigid, protective structure. He works from a corner desk, the only place he feels he can monitor all entry points to the room. The precision of his work, which once brought him satisfaction, is now a battleground. His hand trembles when he tries to draw a clean vector line. He’ll stare at a client’s brief for hours, the words blurring, his mind replaying a loop of tactical lights and shouting voices. He finds himself obsessively checking the locks on his door and windows. He lives in a state of constant, low-grade vigilance, waiting for a threat that has already come and gone, but which for him, has never truly left.
